Aggregation.description:
aggregationSchema :210 — a discriminated union on `function`. row_count takes
no field; the other two require at least one, of different types.

This nesting is why the rule expresses cleanly here but not on the alert
document: the alert format flattens it to sibling value_operation + fields,
where the same constraint would need a cross-field check.

The arms carry `...` for the same reason every other struct here does. The
`*{function: "row_count"}` DEFAULT at each use site stays closed and exact —
it is a concrete instance rather than a type, and a document with extra
members matches these arms instead.

AlertColorPreference.description: Whether a status count is coloured by its text or by a filled background.

AlertDisplayFormat.description:
What the summary widget shows: the status counts, the rules behind them, or
both.

AlertFilters.description:
Rule selections for the summary widget, keyed by facet group — the same shape
the alerts page's filter store holds and the same wire encoding it sends to
/alerts/rules/facets.

Not enumerated, for the reason #SloFilters is not: the facet groups are the
API's to decide, an unknown key is inert on both sides, and closing this
would reject a document the browser round-trips happily.

AlertQuery.description:
An alert query names an alert rule and the widget to draw it as.

A query rather than a member of #PanelConfig for the reason #SloQuery is: it
answers "what data", and #PanelConfig is presentation shared by every panel
type.

Like the slo arm, this one is NOT sent to /explore/query. The webapp fetches
the alert endpoints directly — the rule and its instances for "graph" and
"value", /alerts/rules/stats and /alerts/rules/facets for "summary".

Flat and discriminated only by selectedMode, like its siblings. `ruleId` is
meaningless to "summary" and `filters` to the two widgets that name one rule;
each renderer reads only what its own widget defines.

filters.description: Scopes "summary". Ignored by the widgets that name one rule.

ruleId.description:
The rule "graph" and "value" draw. "" means none picked yet, which the
webapp renders as an empty panel rather than fetching.

ruleName.description:
The rule's name AS IT WAS when the panel was saved. A cache, not an
identifier — ruleId is what names the rule.

Persisted so an editor can label its picker before the lookup returns, and
so a DELETED rule can still be named rather than shown as a bare uuid.
Readers must prefer the live name: a rename would otherwise leave every
dashboard asserting the old one forever.

summaryType.description:
Scopes "summary" like `filters`. Defaults to "monitor", which is what the
widget did before this field existed — an older saved panel keeps its
behaviour rather than silently changing what each row means.

AlertSummaryType.description:
What one row of the summary widget stands for. Mirrors Datadog's
summary_type, with one deliberate difference in what "group" can show.

  monitor  — one row per RULE, carrying that rule's overall state.
  group    — one row per firing INSTANCE of a rule. A rule that groups by
             `pod` fires once per breaching pod, and each is its own row.
  combined — one row per rule, as "monitor", plus a per-state count of that
             rule's instances beside it.

The difference: Datadog's "group" also lists groups that are OK, because a
multi-alert monitor enumerates its groups whether or not they breach. Our
engine materialises an instance only while it is firing, so a healthy series
has no row to show. "group" here therefore means "firing instances", which is
what a dashboard is asking about anyway.

AlertVizType.description: How the graph widget draws the rule's own query. Mirrors Datadog's viz_type.

AlertWidgetType.description:
Which widget an alert query draws.

Datadog's fourth, Check Status, is deliberately absent. It reports OK, Warn,
Alert and No Data; the rule engine persists "normal" and "firing", carries no
warning threshold, and treats no-data as a policy for what to do rather than
a state it observed. Declaring the arm before the data exists is how the
"trend" column cell type came to be accepted by the contract and drawn by
nothing — see #ColumnCellType in config.cue.

value with an inline bar sized against the column's range.

side implemented them. Removed rather than left standing: a schema that
accepts a value nothing renders invites a preset the API stores and the app
then draws as an ordinary number. Re-add it with the renderer, not before.

How a column picks its colours. "conditions" evaluates the rule list in
order; "range" maps the column's values onto a continuous palette.

where it is sent as required_fields. Lenient, like #Field.

ColumnFormat.description:
Formatting for ONE table column.

`id` is a uuid the form uses as its field-array key; `columnId` is the column
it applies to. A columnId matching nothing currently rendered is not an error
— the entry simply does not apply, which is what lets a saved panel survive a
query being edited.

`displayName` is the outermost of four ways to name a column and the one that
wins, over `alignColumns[].displayName` for a merged dimension,
`queries[].columnFields[].alias` for a list column, and
`queries[].labelOptions.format` for a value column, then the field catalog's
label, then the raw key. An EMPTY or whitespace-only value counts as absent
and falls through, so clearing the input restores the derived name instead of
rendering a blank header.

`conditions` judges numbers and `stringConditions` text. Two lists rather
than one mixed list because the rules have different shapes and different
pickers, and because a column carries whichever list its kind offers: both
survive a query edit that changes the kind, and the list that no longer
applies matches nothing and stays stored, so switching the query back
restores the rules.

ColumnPalette.description:
Two families of six. The GRADIENT family ramps from transparent at the
minimum to full colour at the maximum, so a low cell reads as an ordinary row
and only high cells draw the eye. The SOLID family carries full colour across
the whole range, for when every cell should be legible as a band.

For the two-hue ramps the name states the direction: "red-green" is red at
the MINIMUM and green at the maximum. Reversing it is a matter of swapping
min/max, so there is no separate "green-red".

ColumnRange.description:
Continuous colouring across the column's values. `min`/`max` are null for
"derive it from the data", which is the default and what the UI shows as
"auto".

ColumnScale.description:
How a value's position in [min, max] is computed.

"linear" spreads the palette evenly, which is right for bounded values like a
percentage. It is a poor fit for the counts this product mostly shows: those
are power-law distributed, so with a max three orders of magnitude above the
median every row but the largest lands within a few percent of the minimum and
the column reads as blank.

"logarithmic" spreads by order of magnitude instead, and is the DEFAULT for
that reason: a count column is the common case here, and on a linear ramp it
renders as blank cells and one coloured row.

It is computed over log(1 + v), so a range starting at zero — which any count
column with an idle series has — still spreads properly instead of silently
behaving linearly. Only a NEGATIVE minimum falls back to linear, log being
genuinely undefined there.

Condition.description:
One colouring rule. The LAST condition a value satisfies wins, in list
order — not the most specific and not the first. Two rules can overlap
(`> 10` and `> 15`), the user controls the order, so the tie-break has to be
stated rather than discovered.

Last rather than first because a threshold list reads as escalating: rules
get added as the bar rises, so `> 10 green` above `> 15 red` paints 58 red.
This said first-wins until 2026-08-14, under which the general rule shadowed
every more specific rule below it and the severe one could never fire.

A cell whose value is not a number never satisfies a condition.

color.description:
Read only when `style` is "custom-background" or "custom-text". Free-form
like #Threshold.color — the picker emits arbitrary hex.

ConditionStyle.description:
The "show with" choices. The three families (solid background, light
background, coloured text) are spelled out rather than composed from
colour × treatment, because that is how they are presented and because a
composed pair would allow combinations the picker never offers.

The two `custom-*` values are the only ones that read `color`.
The middle severity here is YELLOW, while the range palettes below use
ORANGE. That split is deliberate and matches Datadog: a condition paints a
discrete severity, where yellow reads as "warning" between red and green; a
palette is a continuous ramp, where orange sits better beside red.

CustomColorScheme.description:

codes (#rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa) so callers can drive semantic colours
such as alert severity, and requires at least one.

CustomVariable.description:
A fixed option list authored with the dashboard. At least one option is
required — a picker with nothing in it cannot be resolved.

DefaultPanelConfig.description:

`config` above keeps the #PanelConfig arm intact on export.

filters.description: Which events to mark, written like an events query's filters.

name.description: Label shown in the legend and on the marker's hover card.

EventsQuery.description:
Custom events (deploys, CI runs, incidents) from kube_events.custom_events.
Same query model as logs, so the same base. An advanced filter is stored as
the WHERE text under `filters.advanced_query` with filterMode
"ADVANCED_QUERY"; its fields are the events catalog and `@key` reads an
attribute.

filterMode keeps the base's full enum although the API serves no SPL or SQL
over events: the zod arm accepts all four, and narrowing here alone would put
this contract and the editor's schema in disagreement.

Field.description:
#Field mirrors fieldSchema :185. `type` is a plain string, not an enum — the
engine resolves names and types against its own catalog, so constraining it
would reject spellings the engine accepts.

This is the ONE field definition; everything below narrows it at the point of
use, exactly as the zod does. The narrowing variants build on #FieldBase
rather than on #Field, so they do not inherit #Field's lenient `type` default
onto a member they then make required — required-and-defaulted is a
contradiction, and scripts/check-export.mjs now fails the build on it.

is_attribute.description: Whether this is an attribute field.

type.description:
The data type of the field. Defaults to "string" rather than being
required, because stored rules genuinely arrive without it — a live traces
rule with 119 firing series carries
`groupBy: [{field: "workload", is_attribute: false}]` and no type at all.
Requiring it rejected a document the product itself wrote and is running.

"string" is the safe fill: a group-by key is a string, and the two places a
NUMERIC type is load-bearing declare their own, so an aggregation cannot
silently acquire a string column.

FieldConfig.description:
fieldConfig — per-query display overrides, present on every arm of the
union (queryFieldConfigSchema). Named after Grafana's fieldConfig: a
"field" is a result column or series, and this is how that field displays,
as opposed to the panel-wide `config`.

`unit`: Y_AXIS_FORMATTERS is derived at runtime from the unit cascader, so
its own zod resolves to plain string and so does this.

`color`: the query's own colour, outranking the panel `colorScheme` for
every series the query yields (threshold colours still outrank it). Two
arms, sharing the panel scheme's vocabulary (queryColorOverrideSchema):
  - single  — one hex colour; a grouped query that returns several series
              is drawn in shades of it rather than all identical
  - palette — a named palette cycled from `offset`, restarting at 0 for
              this query rather than continuing the panel counter

Filters.description:
uiStoreFilterSchema (types/zod/filter.ts:3) — the editor's filter store shape,
key to list of values. The zod's .catch({}) default is applied at each use
site, not here.

See the EMPTY-CONTAINER DEFAULT rule at the bottom of this file: a constrained
type must be a NAMED definition whenever an empty default sits beside it.

FloatOrStringField.description:

string column is valid too. Explicit, same reason as #FloatField.

HostMapColor.description:
One host map level's colours: a table column's range, plus `reverse`, which
flips the palette end for end. Every two-hue palette is red at the minimum,
so without it "high CPU is red" could not be said.

InfrastructureDimension.description:
Canonical dimensions every result row is labelled with, whichever metric
family (k8s or legacy) answered it.

InfrastructureEntity.description:
The fixed nesting a host map draws, outermost first. A level list follows
this order; kubeapi rejects one that does not.

InfrastructureFilters.description:
Values per dimension, matched exactly. Container is absent: no metric that
places a container also names its host, so it could not narrow the levels
around it.

advanced_query.description: The Advanced filter's expression, one entry, as logs queries store it.

InfrastructureQuery.description:
A host map's query: up to three nested levels sharing one filter and one
grouping. Like the slo and alert arms it is NOT sent to /explore/query; the
webapp posts it to /explore/hostmap, which compiles it to PromQL per level
and per metric family. A filter value with a leading "-" excludes.

filterMode.description:
"ADVANCED_QUERY" when the filter is a WHERE-style expression, held in
filters.advanced_query as logs queries hold theirs, e.g.
  namespace = "payments" AND (cluster = "prod" OR cluster = "staging")
Fields are the filter dimensions; operators are =, != and IN, with AND,
OR, NOT and parentheses. NOT is a prefix: exclude a list as
NOT namespace IN (a, b).

groupByDimensions.description:
Sections around the outermost level's tiles. Only dimensions that level
carries are accepted by kubeapi; a host has no namespace. Not `groupBy`,
which the logs and traces arms use for a list of field objects.

InfrastructureSignal.description:
What colours (fill) or sizes (size) a tile. Each entity supports a subset,
checked by kubeapi against its PromQL catalog.

IntervalMacro.description:
Grafana-style interval macros. The API resolves these (observability/
promqlmacros) before execution, the first two against the step the query
actually runs with, $__time_filter against the selected time range, so they
reach VictoriaMetrics as concrete durations and never appear in a stored
query's meaning. Valid anywhere a window literal is.

LabelOptions.description:
labelOptionsSchema :344 — discriminated on `type`, defaulting to auto
(DEFAULT_LABEL_OPTIONS :133).

Three arms for two cases. The first is the concrete default instance, and it
has to be written with plain fields rather than `!` — a required field is
never concrete, so `*#AutoLabelOptions` would leave nothing for the default to
materialise. But a closed concrete arm rejects any member added later, and
unlike `aggregation` or `sortBy` the auto case had no open sibling to fall
through to: `{type: "auto", somethingNew: 1}` matched neither arm. #AutoLabel
is that sibling.

LayoutItem.description:
subGridLayoutItemSchema :122 — one react-grid-layout cell. `i` is the item
key that ties a cell to the thing it positions; x/y are grid coordinates and
w/h are spans, all in grid units rather than pixels.

Every member is required with no default: a cell missing its position is not
something to guess at.

i.description: Identifier linking this cell to what it lays out.

x.description: Column offset from the left edge, in grid units.

y.description: Row offset from the top, in grid units.

The zod adds selectedMode via .extend() on each arm. A CUE definition is
closed, so a field can be narrowed but not introduced by unification — hence
the discriminator is declared here across every arm and narrowed to a literal
below, which reaches the same place.

columnFields.description:
No .catch() on this one in the zod — the only member of the base without a
fallback.

xaxis.description:
SPL/SQL-only visualisation hints (:642-656). "auto" means the formatter
infers the column.

yaxis.description:
yaxis is a LIST, not a string. It was a string until commit 2c8d7ab1a
(2026-08-07, "update y-axis handling to support multiple select"), which
changed the persisted type and added coerceYaxisColumns + yaxisColumnsSchema
(:571, :586) plus a coercion step in migrateToNewSchema (:854) so stored
documents holding `yaxis: "cpu"` keep that selection.

Worth noting what that change cost: it is a breaking type change to a
persisted field, and it is detected by sniffing `!Array.isArray(next.yaxis)`
because panels carry no version marker. With one, the migration would key
off the version instead of guessing from shape.

LogsVariable.description: Same as traces, against the logs store.

filters.description:
Label matchers for builder mode, keyed by label. Each value's prefix picks
its PromQL operator: `v` is `label="v"`, `-v` is `label!="v"`, `~re` is
`label=~"re"` and `-~re` is `label!~"re"`. So `-` alone excludes the empty
value (`label!=""`). A whole `$var` or `-$var` value stands for the
variable's selected values.

is missing and then PERSISTS it on the next save, so an omitted
selectedMetric is not neutral — it silently becomes a real query against an
unrelated metric.

Offset and @ on the series selector. The builder renders them once, where
the selector is first consumed: after its window, as in
`rate(m[5m] offset 1h @ end())`, or after the bare selector when nothing
windows it. Never between a selector and its window, which does not parse.

field, and has NO filterMode — the metrics path has no advanced-query mode.

Same reason as #Filters: an inline constraint arm beside a default is

PaletteScheme.description:

stays closed and exact — it is a concrete instance, not a type — and these
arms are what a real document with an extra member matches instead.

Optional, and blank is meaningful rather than missing. The zod is a bare
z.string() (no .min(1)), and its own description says so: blank means
automatic, with the display title derived from the query at render time
(panel-name.ts) instead of stored. So "" is a real value here, not a
placeholder for one — and a panel that omits the key entirely means the
same thing. Neither is an error; both render a derived title.

No .catch() here either: `queries` must be present. An empty array is
permitted by the shape, though a panel with no queries renders nothing.

columnFormatting.description: Per-column formatting. Table and list panels.

eventOverlay.description:
Event markers on this panel. Absent means inherit the dashboard's.
Timeseries and bar panels only.

hostMapColors.description:
How each host map level is coloured, keyed by entity so removing or
re-adding a level never moves one level's colours onto another. Host map
panels only. A level with no entry gets a neutral ramp.

lineWidth.description:
From graphStyles, flattened into config by the migration at

mergeTables.description:
From tableOptions. The zod is z.literal(true).catch(true) — merging is no
longer optional, so the only legal value is true. Kept because stored
documents carry the key.

step.description:
Query resolution. "auto" lets the range decide; a positive integer forces
a step in seconds.

timeFrame.description:
The window this panel queries instead of the dashboard's time. Absent
means the dashboard's time. Every query the panel makes uses it, and the
panel does not drag-to-zoom.

topListDisplayMode.description: Flat or stacked bars. Top-list panels only.

visualFormattingRules.description:

yAxisLabelFormatter.description:
Y axis. yAxisMin/Max are nullable — null means "auto", a hard number
clamps that end of the axis.

PanelEventOverlay.description:
How a panel picks its event overlays. "inherit" uses the dashboard's,
"custom" uses `overlays` instead (it replaces, never merges), and "off" draws
none.

PanelTimeFrame.description:
PANEL_TIME_FRAME_KEYS — a window relative to now that a panel queries in
place of the dashboard's time. The rolling ones end at now. "week_to_date"
starts Monday 00:00 of the current week and "month_to_date" the 1st 00:00 of
the current month, both ending at now. "previous_week" is the previous Monday
00:00 to Sunday 23:59:59.999 and "previous_month" the 1st to the last day
23:59:59.999 of the previous month. Calendar boundaries fall in the viewer's
timezone. Every value is relative; a panel cannot pin an absolute range.

PanelType.description:
PANEL_TYPES :166 — note "timeSeries" here, camel-cased, versus the query-level
chart_type's "timeseries". Both spellings are real and they are not the same
field.

An "slo" panel names service level objectives rather than running a metrics
query, but it still carries a query: #SloQuery, the `slo` arm of the query
union, which holds the widget type and which objectives to draw.

(An earlier revision kept that selection in #PanelConfig and left `queries`
empty. It moved because the selection answers "what data", which is what a
query is.)

An "alert" panel works the same way and for the same reason: #AlertQuery
names a rule and the widget to draw it as, and is served by the alert
endpoints rather than /explore/query.

A "hostMap" panel carries one #InfrastructureQuery, which /explore/hostmap
compiles to PromQL server-side, so the panel never holds PromQL of its own.

A "syntheticsMonitor" panel carries one #SyntheticsMonitorQuery and is
served by the synthetics endpoints, as an "slo" panel is by the SLO ones.

QueryFunctions.description:
── the EMPTY-CONTAINER DEFAULT rule ────────────────────────────────────────

`*{} | <inline constrained type>` and `*[] | <inline constrained type>` both
LOSE the constraint on export. The empty container subsumes the other arm, CUE
reduces the disjunction to its default, and the encoder emits `const: {}` or a
bare `{"type": "array"}` — silently, with no error and no $defs entry.

This is not cosmetic. `functions: *[] | [...#QueryFunction]` exported as
`{"type": "array"}`, so the entire six-variant builder-function catalog —
argument names, tuple arities, every enum — validated nothing at all. Naming
the arm and referencing it keeps both arms as an anyOf.

So: any type that appears beside an empty default gets a name below.

Range's `over` has always been an open string and stays one; rollup's is
constrained to a macro or a duration literal.

RollupTimeRange.description:
A rollup window. Once an enum of six literals the builder offered; widened to
any duration so a typed window like `15m` is accepted, and to #IntervalMacro
because the macros are as valid a rollup window as any literal.

RumQuery.description:

RumVariable.description:

RUM filter. Applying it is an ordinary field filter. rumEventType is required
with no default, like #RumQuery: without it there is no table to read (the UI
picks "view" when it authors one, but a stored variable must say so).

SelectorModifiers.description:
`offset` shifts the lookbehind back by a duration; `at` pins evaluation to
the query's start(), its end() or a unix timestamp in seconds.

SloFilters.description:
SLO filter selections, keyed by filter field — the shape the webapp's filter
store holds, not the converted request body. The conversion expands dashboard
variables and drops unresolved ones, so it is lossy and depends on where it
ran; the panel stores what was picked and converts when it queries.

Not enumerated. The SLO filter API decides which fields exist, and an unknown
key is inert on both sides, so closing this would reject a document the
browser round-trips happily.

SloQuery.description:
An slo query names service level objectives and the widget to draw them as.

It is a query rather than a member of #PanelConfig because it answers "what
data" — which is what every other arm of this union answers too. #PanelConfig
is presentation, shared by all ten panel types.

Unlike every other arm this one is NOT sent to /explore/query. The webapp
excludes it and fetches from /slo/list and /slo/stats instead.

Flat, discriminated only by selectedMode like its siblings. `widgetType` is a
plain enum rather than a nested union because CUE exports a union-of-unions
as an intersection of open structs, losing the narrowing that makes the
discriminant worth having. The cost is that `objectiveId` is meaningless
outside "single" and the table fields outside "list"; each renderer reads
only what its own widget defines.

filters.description: Scopes "summary" and "list". Ignored by "single", which names one SLO.

objectiveId.description:
The objective "single" draws. "" means none picked yet, which the webapp
renders as an empty panel rather than fetching.

objectiveName.description:
The objective's name AS IT WAS when the panel was saved. A cache, not an
identifier — objectiveId is what names the SLO.

Persisted so an editor can label its picker before the lookup returns, and
so a DELETED objective can still be named rather than shown as a bare
uuid. Readers must prefer the live name: a rename would otherwise leave
every dashboard asserting the old one forever.

showErrorBudget.description:
Show each window's remaining error budget beside its compliance. Both
numbers are already on every SLO row, so this costs no extra request.

timeWindows.description:
Which rollup windows "single" draws.

These four and no others, because these are the four the API computes.
getSLOMetricsForSLOs builds one CTE per window with a literal INTERVAL, so
the set is fixed server-side rather than parameterised — a document naming
"90 days" would describe a column no response carries. Widen this only
together with the query and the columns.

"last_28_days" is four whole weeks, deliberately not 30 days.

viewMode.description:
What "single" draws: the objective's own rollups, a per-group breakdown,
or both. Only meaningful for a GROUPED objective — the webapp falls back
to the rollups when a panel names an SLO with no groups, so a saved
document does not blank itself if its SLO changes shape.

widgetType.description:
"single", not "summary": an unconfigured panel waits for an objective
rather than fetching a fleet-wide rollup nobody asked for. The webapp
moved to that default in #2388 and this side was missed, so a panel saved
without the field meant one widget to the browser and another to
ApplyDefaults. The two must agree — this is the number the published
schema hands every other consumer.

SloSortField.description:
The fields an SLO list can be ordered by. Only these two sort: /slo/list
builds its ORDER BY from this, and an SLO's compliance and error budget are
computed after that query returns, so there is no column for them. "" is
unsorted.

SloTableView.description:
Which layout the list widget draws.

Only "primary" reads from the row the list already returned. The other three
fetch a timeline per row through a queue shared by every SLO table in the
browser, so a dashboard of them would contend with each other and with the
SLO page. All four are legal so enabling them later is a renderer change
rather than a contract change.

SloTimeWindow.description: The rollup windows the API computes for every SLO.

SloWidgetType.description: Which widget an slo query draws.

StringCondition.description:
One "if the text is X, then ..." rule, for STRING columns. The counterpart
of #Condition, kept as its own definition for the reason #VisualFormattingRule
is: the two share the "show with" vocabulary and nothing else. A threshold
compares numbers and always paints; a string rule compares text and has TWO
optional effects, so it may paint, replace, or both. Widening
#Condition.value to `number | string` was considered and rejected: it would
let a "contains" rule carry a number and a ">" rule carry text, and the
editor would have to guess which picker to show.

`style` is absent when "Show with" is unchecked, and `replace` when "Replace"
is. A rule with neither is legal and inert, for the reason
#VisualFormattingRule.color gives: a conditional requirement costs the zod
its totality.

The two effects resolve DIFFERENTLY, and the asymmetry is deliberate.

The fill takes the LAST matching rule that has a style, in list order, the
same tie-break as #Condition: a cell has one colour, so one rule has to win,
and last-wins lets the list read as escalating.

The replacement is a PIPELINE: EVERY matching rule's replace applies, in
list order, each on the output of the rule before it. Last-wins was
considered here too and rejected because text composes where colour does
not. Under last-wins a `starts-with "/api"` prefix-strip written below a
`contains "v1"` rewrite would silently cancel the rule above it, with
nothing in the editor saying so. Chaining means two substring rules
compose and a later "cell" replace overwrites whatever the earlier rules
produced, which is what the order on screen suggests. Each rule is still
JUDGED against the cell's original text, not the text the rules before it
produced; only the replacement input chains. Judging the rewritten text
would let a rule's own output stop it matching.

Only a cell whose raw value is a string is judged. A number is left to
#Condition, and a cell that is not text is never painted or rewritten by
these rules. When a column carries both lists they evaluate as one
sequence, `conditions` then `stringConditions`; the two can only both
match a numeric-looking string such as "404", and the string list sitting
later means it wins there, which is the more specific statement about
that column.

color.description:
Read only when `style` is "custom-background" or "custom-text", and
optional even then, for the reason #VisualFormattingRule.color gives.

style.description:
Any of the eleven #ConditionStyle values. OPTIONAL, unlike
#Condition.style, because painting is one of two effects here and the
checkbox that enables it can be off.

value.description:
An EMPTY value matches NOTHING under the six operators that read it. It is
a rule that has not been written yet, not a rule about the empty string:
four of them are otherwise true for every cell, since every string starts
with, ends with and contains "", and "is-not" holds for any non-empty one.
Left alone, adding a rule would paint the whole column before stating a
predicate. #Condition has no such state to guard, being seeded with a real
number.

"is-empty" and "is-not-empty" ignore this field, which is what lets
emptiness be asked about without colliding with the unfinished state.

StringConditionOperator.description:
How a string rule compares the cell's text to `value`. Case-sensitive: the
text a rule names is the text the cell shows, and "is" should mean is.

"is-empty" and "is-not-empty" read NO `value` at all, and exist because the
other six cannot express emptiness. An empty `value` is reserved to mean "a
rule not written yet" (see #StringCondition.value), so `is-not` with a blank
cannot be "the cell has text" — the two readings are indistinguishable on
screen, and the unfinished one is far commoner. Naming the intent settles it:
the operator says emptiness is the subject, and the value input disappears.

StringReplace.description:
What a string rule writes into the cell in place of its text. Two arms on
`mode`, like #ColorScheme on `type`, because they take different inputs:
"cell" swaps the WHOLE text for `with`; "substring" swaps every occurrence
of `search` for `with`. A union rather than one struct with an optional
`search` so that a "cell" replace cannot carry a search string that
nothing reads. A "substring" arm whose `search` is empty replaces nothing,
there being no occurrence of nothing to find, rather than salting `with`
between every character.

An empty `with` means different things in the two arms, and the split is
deliberate. Under "substring" it DELETES the match, which is how a prefix is
stripped. Under "cell" it is INERT rather than blanking the cell: the editor
seeds an empty `with` the moment "Replace" is ticked, so writing it through
would empty every matching cell before anything had been typed, which reads
as data loss. Blanking a cell outright is the rarer intent and a single
space expresses it.

SubGrid.description:
subGridSchema :130 — a collapsible group holding its own panels and its own
layout. Note the nesting is one level only: a sub-grid contains panels, never
further sub-grids.

collapsed.description: Whether the group is folded shut in the UI.

gridLayout.description: Positions for this group's own panels.

panels.description:
Panels belonging to this group, laid out by gridLayout below rather than by
the dashboard's top-level layout.

SyntheticsCheckType.description: The synthetics check types, as synthetics-api spells them.

showApdex.description:
Show each monitor's apdex (0 to 1) beside its uptime. Apdex is null for
a monitor whose runs in the range carry no apdex threshold.

SyntheticsMonitorFilter.description:
Which monitors a panel draws when it does not name them, or how it narrows
the ones it names. Every key present must match; within types and within
states any one value matches.

Labels are a map here and a list of "key:value" on the wire: the renderer
sends them as `labels` to POST /api/synthetics/uptimes. Types go as `types`.
That endpoint does not filter by state, so a states filter is resolved
through GET /api/synthetics/monitors?state=…, which carries each monitor's
state, and the uptimes are then fetched for the ids it returns.

SyntheticsMonitorIds.description:
At most 100 monitors: the cap POST /api/synthetics/uptimes enforces, which
answers a longer list with a 422 rather than truncating it.

SyntheticsMonitorLabels.description: Monitor labels to match, key to value. Every pair must match.

SyntheticsMonitorQuery.description:
A synthetics_monitor query names synthetics monitors and the widget to draw
them as. Not "synthetics": that selectedMode is the Explore source over the
synthetics results, a log-like query run through /explore/query.

A query rather than a member of #PanelConfig for the reason #SloQuery is: it
answers "what data".

Like the slo and alert arms, this one is NOT sent to /explore/query. The
webapp posts the selection to /api/synthetics/uptimes and, for "single",
reads the state counts from /api/synthetics/monitors/summary (or, when the
panel selects monitors, from the states of the monitors it selects).

The panel names monitors by `monitorIds`, selects them by `filter`, or
both, in which case the filter narrows the named ones. With neither it draws
every monitor, the first 100 by name.

Flat, discriminated only by selectedMode, with `widgetType` a plain enum,
for the reason #SloQuery gives.

monitorIds.description:
The monitors to draw, in display order unless display.sort says
otherwise. An id that no longer exists is reported by the API and
skipped.

widgetType.description:
Required: this arm has no stored documents that predate it, so there
is no older panel for a default to keep drawing.

window.description:
The window the uptime covers, ending now. Absent, the panel's time range
applies: its config.timeFrame, else the dashboard's.

SyntheticsMonitorState.description: A monitor's presented state. PAUSED is a disabled monitor.

SyntheticsQuery.description:
Synthetic check runs from kube_synthetics.synthetics_results, one row per
run. Same query model as logs, so the same base, and served by
/explore/query and /explore/query-range like events. Fields are the
synthetics results catalog; `@key` reads a run attribute and
`labels.<key>` a monitor label.

Not "synthetics_monitor", the arm that names monitors and is served by the
synthetics endpoints rather than /explore.

No narrowing beyond the base, for the reason #EventsQuery gives: the zod
arm is the base extended with this literal, and narrowing here alone would
put this contract and the editor's schema in disagreement.

SyntheticsSortField.description:
How rows are ordered. Unset, they keep the order the API returned: the
order of monitorIds when the panel names monitors, by name otherwise.

SyntheticsUptimeThresholds.description:
Uptime percentages a monitor is coloured by: at or above `good` is healthy,
at or above `warn` a warning, below it failing.

SyntheticsUptimeWindow.description: The uptime windows synthetics-api computes, each ending now.

SyntheticsWidgetType.description:
Which widget a synthetics_monitor query draws.

  uptime      — one row per selected monitor: its uptime over the window,
                coloured against display.thresholds, with apdex beside it
                when display.showApdex.
  status_list — one row per selected monitor carrying its current state
                (UP, DOWN, …) beside its uptime.
  single      — one figure for the whole selection: its uptime (runs
                succeeded over runs made) with the selection's state counts.

Tab.description:
One tab: an id and a title, plus a page of its own. A page is the same four
members the untabbed top level carries — panels, gridLayout, subGrids and
subGridLayout — so a tab can hold rows.

Every tab rule lives in schema/tabs.go, not here, because each is refused for
every origin, including the UI's own save, where an ordinary contract finding
is only logged. That covers the id (stable, used in the ?tab= URL: 1 to 40
lowercase letters, digits or dashes, unique) and the title (not blank, at
most 50 characters, unique ignoring case), as well as the top-level page
staying empty, sub-grid ids unique across tabs, and one layout cell per panel.

TableSettings.description:
Table-level state that survives a panel save, for the table and list panels.
Every key after `columnWidths` is a TanStack Table state slice under its own
name and shape, so the persisted value is handed to `useReactTable` as-is.

columnPinning.description: `ColumnPinningState`: column ids pinned to each edge, in order.

columnVisibility.description: `VisibilityState`: column id → shown. Absent ids are visible.

columnWidths.description:
Per-column pixel widths, keyed by column id. (TanStack calls this
`columnSizing`; the name predates the rule above and renaming needs a
migration.)

sorting.description: `SortingState`: applied in order, first entry primary.

TextboxVariable.description: A free-text value the viewer types.

color.description:
THRESHOLD_COLORS supplies three presets (red #e24d42, green #56a64b,
orange #ef843c) but the field is a free string — the colour picker emits
arbitrary hex — so it is not enumerated.

ThresholdValue.description:
thresholdOptionsSchema :377. `threshold` is a union of a number with the two
infinity SENTINEL STRINGS — JSON has no Infinity literal, so the zod encodes
them as "-Infinity"/"Infinity" and the default threshold is the negative one,
meaning "from the bottom of the range".

TopListDisplayMode.description:
TOP_LIST_DISPLAY_MODES — top-list panels only. "stacked" splits each row's bar
by the group-bys after the first, so it needs two or more of them. The webapp
renders "flat" regardless when the data carries a single dimension, which
makes a stored "stacked" on a one-group-by panel stale rather than invalid —
hence no cross-field rule here.

TracesVariable.description: Values discovered by querying the traces store for a field's distinct values.

filterMode.description:
Only MFD and ADVANCED_QUERY here — a variable cannot be driven by an SPL or
SQL query, unlike a panel query's filterMode.

filters.description: Narrows which rows the distinct values are drawn from.

TransformArg.description:
The only legacy shape that is a plain array rather than a fixed tuple: abs,
sort and the math functions take none, clamp takes two, the rest take one,
and the arm accepted any of the four names on any transform.

ValueCalculation.description:
VALUE_CALCULATION_OPTIONS — likewise built at runtime from the options map.
These reduce the per-bucket values of a stat panel. "Whole range" is not a
member: it is the absence of a calculation (see #ValueOptions), so there is
one way to say it.

ValueOptions.description:
`show` has a single legal value; the field exists so a future "hide" mode is
additive rather than a shape change.

calculation.description:
Optional on purpose. Absent means the number is computed over the whole
range in one aggregate for ClickHouse-backed sources (rum, logs, traces,
events, synthetics), so a unique count or percentile is exact; metrics
panels use the last value. Any value set here instead reduces the
per-bucket values.

Variable.description:
dashboardVariableSchema :42. `meta` is a discriminated union on
`variableType`, so the outer object carries only name/description.

description.description:
Required with no default in the zod, so an empty string is valid but the
key must be present.

name.description:
Referenced in queries as $name. The regex is the zod's own: must start with
a letter or underscore, then letters, digits and underscores only, max 20
characters — so it is safe to substitute into PromQL and filter values
without escaping.

VariableField.description:
The field a datasource-backed variable draws its values from. Structurally the
same three members as the panel package's #Field, but restated because the zod
declares it inline per variant (:68, :85, :105) with a non-empty field name
rather than reusing fieldSchema.

VisualFormattingRule.description:
One "if the value is X, paint the block Y" rule, for top-list and stat panels.

Deliberately the same shape as #Condition, down to LAST-MATCH-WINS: the two
are the same idea on different surfaces, and one vocabulary means one picker
and one thing to explain. Kept as its own definition rather than a reuse of
#Condition because the style set is narrower and because `id` is required
here — the form uses it as a field-array key.

Every block is judged by ITS OWN value, so on a stacked row the rule marks
the block that breached rather than the whole bar.

Supersedes `thresholds` for top-list panels, which no longer offer the
Thresholds section, and for stat panels, which no longer offer it either. A
panel saved before this existed has an empty list and keeps being coloured
by its thresholds; the first rule added moves it over.

color.description:
Read only when `style` is "custom-background", and OPTIONAL even then: a
custom rule with no colour is INERT, painting nothing, rather than an
error. Deliberate, and the same stance #Condition takes.

Requiring it here was considered and rejected. The zod cannot mirror a
conditional requirement without a .refine, which would cost the rule
schema its TOTALITY — and `visualFormattingRules` carries a `.catch([])`,
so one refusable entry would take every valid sibling rule with it on
read. Requiring it on this side alone is worse still: the browser would
accept a document the API rejects, which is the drift
`conformance.test.ts` exists to catch, and the editor would build panels
that cannot be saved.

The editor closes the gap where it opens: choosing "Custom background"
seeds a colour immediately, so the half-configured state is not reachable
from the UI. What remains is a hand- or agent-written preset saying
"custom" and meaning nothing, which renders as though the rule were absent.

VisualFormattingStyle.description:
The styles a visual formatting rule may carry: the whole #ConditionStyle
set. A stat panel paints its block solid or light, or colours its value
text, so every family applies there. A top-list block only has a background
and sits beside blocks in their series colour, where a solid fill reads as
another series — so the top-list PICKER offers the light backgrounds and
custom only. That narrowing lives in the editor, not here: the contract
accepts every style on both surfaces, and a solid style on a top list is
simply drawn as the fill it names.

YaxisColumns.description:
yaxisColumnsSchema :586 — a non-empty list of column names. Named rather than
inlined so the min-length survives export alongside the default.

description:
dashboardPresetSchema :140.

gridLayout and panels are required with no .catch(); everything else defaults
to empty. On a tabbed dashboard both are empty and each tab carries its own
page instead. Panels at the top level are positioned by gridLayout; panels inside
a sub-grid are positioned by that sub-grid's own gridLayout, and subGridLayout
positions the sub-grids themselves.

eventOverlays.description:
Event markers drawn on every timeseries and bar panel that inherits them.
Absent means none.

publicDashboardPath.description:
Set when the dashboard has been shared publicly; the path the public view
is served at.

schema_version.description:
The document's schema version, and the entry point for migration. A reader
migrates from whatever version the document was saved at up to
CurrentVersion, one step at a time, then renders — which is what lets ONE
renderer display dashboards written years apart.

Versioned at the DOCUMENT level, not per panel. A nested panel carries no
version of its own; the preset's chain migrates its panels as part of
migrating the preset. Grafana does the same: schemaVersion sits on the
dashboard and DashboardMigrator reaches into panels from there. Versioning
panels independently would mean a document whose parts are at different
versions, and no single number to key a migration off.

Absent means LEGACY, which is version 0 — NOT 1. Every dashboard already
stored predates this field, so it is the one population guaranteed never
to have been checked against this contract; calling it v1 would assert a
shape it does not have. `legacy -> v1` is a real step with a real
transform (migrate/dashboard), not a version the chain pretends happened.

The default below is what a document gets STAMPED with, and it must equal
the Go chain's CurrentVersion — this is the second place that number is
written, and TestGeneratedDefaultVersionMatchesTheChain is what stops the
two drifting. Bump both together.

subGridLayout.description: Positions for the sub-grids within the dashboard.

subGrids.description: Collapsible groups, each with its own panels and layout.

tabs.description:
Tabs, each with a page of its own. Empty or absent means the dashboard is
untabbed and its page is the top level above. When non-empty, the
top-level panels, gridLayout, subGrids and subGridLayout must all be
empty; they stay present so an older reader still parses the document.
Variables, event overlays and publicDashboardPath stay at the top level
and apply to every tab.
